nameStory: The Western Sandpiper gets its name from its main breeding grounds in western Alaska and Siberia, even though it migrates along both coasts of North America. The scientific name 'mauri' honors Italian botanist Ernesto Mauri, while 'Calidris' comes from an ancient Greek word Aristotle used for grey waterside birds. It's a bit confusing that this 'western' bird shows up regularly on our eastern shores!
description: The Western Sandpiper is a small, energetic shorebird about the size of a sparrow that visits New England during migration. These compact birds have brownish-grey backs with darker streaks, white bellies, and relatively long, slightly drooping black bills. They're one of the most abundant shorebirds in North America, traveling thousands of miles between their Arctic breeding grounds and wintering areas. You'll often see them scurrying along the water's edge in small flocks, busily probing the sand and mud for tiny creatures.

idTips.label: Bill shape and length
idTips.description: Look for a black bill that's noticeably longer than the head and droops slightly at the tip, like a tiny tweezers - this drooping tip is key for distinguishing from very similar sandpipers

idTips.label: Rusty breeding colors
idTips.description: In spring and early summer, adults show distinctive rusty-red patches on the crown, ear coverts, and back that catch the light beautifully - much more colorful than their plain winter plumage

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Watch for rapid, almost frantic probing motions as they stick their bills deep into wet sand and mud, often submerging their entire head while feeding

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Black legs that appear sturdy relative to their small body size, clearly visible as they run quickly along the water's edge

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Compact and stocky for a small sandpiper, about 6-7 inches long with a somewhat chunky appearance compared to the more delicate look of similar species

habitat: Western Sandpipers visit New England's coastal mudflats, sandy beaches, and salt marsh edges during spring and fall migration. Look for them at popular birding spots like Plum Island in Massachusetts or along the Connecticut coast, especially where retreating tides expose rich feeding areas. They prefer areas with soft substrate where they can easily probe for marine worms, small crustaceans, and other invertebrates.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs in May, when adults in bright rusty breeding plumage pass through on their way to Arctic nesting grounds. This is the best time to see their distinctive rufous coloring and practice identification.
seasonality.summer: Very few remain in New England during summer, as most are on northern breeding grounds. Any spotted are likely non-breeding individuals or early fall migrants.
seasonality.fall: July through September brings waves of migrants, including many juveniles with fresh, crisp plumage. Adults in duller fall plumage can be more challenging to identify.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in New England winters, as most birds continue south to warmer coastal areas from the mid-Atlantic to South America.

funFact: Western Sandpipers can make one of the longest nonstop flights in the animal kingdom - some individuals fly directly from Alaska to South America, covering over 4,000 miles without landing, burning half their body weight as fuel during the journey!
confusionNotes: Western Sandpipers are notoriously difficult to distinguish from Semipalmated Sandpipers, earning the nickname 'peeps' along with other small, similar sandpipers. The key memory trick: Western Sandpipers have 'western drawl' - their bills are longer and droop at the tip like a cowboy's mustache, while Semipalmated Sandpipers have shorter, straighter bills.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Western' Sandpipers, these birds are regular migrants along the Atlantic coast and are actually more common than Semipalmated Sandpipers in many New England locations during certain times of year. The name simply reflects their breeding distribution, not where you're likely to see them during migration.
compareHints: Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage. Least Sandpipers are smaller with yellowish legs (not black), while Sanderlings are larger, paler, and prefer running along surf lines rather than probing in mudflats. The bill shape remains the most reliable field mark for separating Western from Semipalmated Sandpipers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
